Our format allows each reader 15 minutes to present their work aloud, followed by approximately 20 minutes of feedback from the other attendees. To ensure fairness, each attendee is limited to 1 minute of Initial Feedback time. During that period, the author remains silent. item.title: AI Agents in Survey Research: Foundations, Applications, Oversight, and Evaluation — Tue Feb 23, 10:00 AM
item.description: This course explores the emerging role of AI agents in survey research. Designed for survey practitioners, data scientists, and social scientists, it introduces agentic AI as the next iteration of artificial intelligence technologies to be integrated with survey research methods. Building on foundational concepts in generative AI, the course examines how agents differ from the previous iteration of LLMs and considers their potential uses across the survey research lifecycle. Participants will learn core technical concepts around agentic AI, approaches to evaluating agent performance in the survey context, the challenges of designing, implementing, and assessing agentic workflows, responsible AI deployment, AI-assisted vs AI-driven paradigms of work, and the role of human expertise in survey research. item.title: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage — Tue Feb 23, 10:00 AM — Gregg Museum of Art & Design
item.description:
Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage at the Gregg Museum of Art & Design presents a series of vignettes exploring spaces of dignity, belonging, safety, and imagination within Black communities across North Carolina. Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.
Source: NC Cultural Resources

item.description:
Join the African American Cultural Center to experience ariana Farquharson's You Are Here: Geolocating the Self through the Familiar in the Midst of the Unfamiliar. The exhibition is a speculative, immersive world-building study that invites guests to explore (geo)locating self and home amid a rapidly and frequently changing post-pandemic “new” world. It will be on display in the art gallery at the African American Cultural Center from Oct. 28, 2026, to Feb. 28, 2027. A behind-the-scenes look at the exhibition is set for Nov. 11.
Source: NC State African American Cultural Center

item.title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians — Wed Feb 24 — Presbyterian Heritage Center
item.description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority, and is published that it may go down to posterity.”
The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.
But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting.

The course includes opportunities for educators to learn strategies for using art to identify math concepts, apply math skills to create art, and to reflect within a collaborative peer learning community. Participants will gain an understanding of best practices in arts integration and will become more familiar with the North Carolina Museum of Art’s collection.
Each course module is divided into three sections: Define, Explore, and Practice. In Define, we introduce concepts, vocabulary, and works of art to stimulate thinking and help you begin identifying points of integration between art and math. item.title: DQC Seminar Series: An End-to-End Approach to the Challenges in Photonic Integrated Circuits (PIC) and Packaging — Tue Dec 1, 12:00 PM — None
item.description: AIM Photonics, a Department of War Manufacturing Innovation Institute (DoW MII), offers end-to-end services spanning photonic integrated circuits (PICs), interposers, heterogeneous integration (HI), electronic-photonic design automation (EPDA), and packaging. AIM Photonics leverages the NY Creates Albany NanoTech Complex, a 300 mm wafer fabrication facility in Albany, NY, and the Test Assembly and Packaging (TAP) facility in Rochester, NY, to provide these state-of-the-art capabilities. As a DoW MII, AIM Photonics' mission is to develop photonics and packaging technologies, make them available to the domestic ecosystem, and train a skilled workforce. This talk will focus on how AIM Photonics is advancing that mission. To help advance the ecosystem, AIM Photonics offers application-specific PIC technologies in 1) base telecom and datacom, 2) SiN sensors, 3) Quantum Flex (QFlex), and 4) III-V heterogeneous integration. The base telecom PIC technology has been offered as an MPW since 2016

item.title: Who Owns Patriot Culture?: Frederick Douglass, Martin R. Delany, and the Roots of Intelligent Patriotism” — Tue Dec 1, 1:30 PM — Smith Warehouse
item.description:
In this talk, Roy examines the emergence and evolution of what he calls "Patriot Culture" in American society, and in particular the ways in which African American political thinkers diagnosed and engaged that culture through the late eighteenth and the first half of the nineteenth century. First, he will examine patriotic imagery produced since the Revolutionary era, showing how it substitutes spectacle for substance, before turning to closely examining the thought of Martin Delany and Frederick Douglass, who jointly diagnose this culture but offer different solutions. While Delany turns to emigration, Douglass develops the virtue of "intelligent patriotism" to demystify the "specious and popular garb of patriotism" that promotes illusory images of a nation. The talk will conclude by tracing Patriot Culture through the Civil War into Reconstruction, considering how responses from those once formally excluded from citizenship can yet renovate our contemporary discourse.
Keidrick Roy

item.title: First Day Hikes: "Hiking Through History" at Vade Mecum — Fri Jan 1, 10:00 AM — Vade Mecum Trail Center Parking Lot
item.description: Start your New Years off with a brisk 2-mile historical hike along the Vade Mecum trails. Your guide will take you through the decades as we walk through the old Camp Sertoma high ropes course, and stroll along the Pelican Pool trail while learning more about the circus animals that once overwintered here. We will cross over century old bridges and learn about the small town that was once set in these hills. See the spectacular glimmering reflections at the Palisades as we visit the old Mineral Springs, whose water was once sold throughout North Carolina. Sites we will also pass along the way are the outdoor amphitheater, Diamond Lake Dam, and the outdoor Chapel of Peace built by the Episcopalian Diocese. The hike will end with a glance of the Historic Vade Mecum Hotel and Chapel of Thanks as we hike past the property that will reopen to the public in 2027. item.title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians — Tue Feb 23 — Presbyterian Heritage Center
item.description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority, and is published that it may go down to posterity.”
The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.
But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting.

Participants will gain an understanding of best practices in arts integration and will become more familiar with the North Carolina Museum of Art’s collection.

In Define, we introduce concepts, vocabulary, and works of art to stimulate thinking and help you begin identifying points of integration between art and math.
